x.A: Amazon Connect is a contact center service and isn't the right tool for marketing SMS messaging with stored replies.
x.B: Pinpoint supports two-way SMS, so users can reply. A journey sends the confirmations, and Pinpoint events streamed to Kinesis can be archived and analyzed for a year.
x.C: SQS is a queue and can't send SMS messages to users or receive their replies.
x.D: SNS can send SMS but a FIFO topic doesn't support SMS delivery, and SNS doesn't give a two-way SMS flow for replies.

x.A: SSE-S3 keys are managed entirely by S3, and you can't configure or see a yearly rotation, so it doesn't show rotation every year.
x.B: A KMS customer managed key with automatic rotation enabled rotates every year with no manual work, and default bucket encryption applies the key to all new objects.
x.C: Rotating the KMS key manually every year adds operational work that automatic rotation avoids.
x.D: Imported key material can't be rotated automatically, and encrypting before upload adds a lot of work.

x.A: DAX speeds up DynamoDB reads. The delay is in the invitation processing application, not DynamoDB reads.
x.B: An API Gateway in front of the web application doesn't speed up the sending of meeting invitations from the queue.
x.C: CloudFront in front of the web application won't change how fast the queue is processed.
x.D: The queue is building up because the invitation application can't keep up. An Auto Scaling group that scales on SQS queue depth adds consumers when the backlog grows, which cuts the delay.

x.A: Moving all the purchase data into RDS is a big change and RDS access controls aren't fine-grained for analytics across a data lake.
x.B: Copying RDS data to S3 with Lambda and using S3 policies means maintaining the copy jobs, and S3 policies aren't fine-grained down to columns and rows.
x.C: Lake Formation builds a data lake over S3 and RDS (through a Glue JDBC connection), and its access controls give fine-grained permissions. It's managed, so operational overhead is low.
x.D: A Redshift cluster with scheduled Lambda copy jobs adds a cluster to manage and custom jobs to maintain.

x.A: A Lightsail server is a single server you manage, so it's less resilient and costs more than S3 for static content.
x.B: EC2 with an Auto Scaling group and an ALB is resilient but costs far more than S3 for a static site.
x.C: A private S3 bucket reachable only by CloudFront through an OAI is very cheap and resilient. Content can be uploaded with the AWS CLI.
x.D: A public bucket exposes the content directly, bypassing CloudFront, and Transfer for SFTP adds ongoing cost that isn't needed.

x.A: A Lambda function that queries CloudTrail logs means writing code and polling, which is more work than a rule.
x.B: Using SNS with CloudTrail log delivery, Athena tables, and queries is several pieces to build and maintain and isn't a real-time alert.
x.C: An EventBridge rule matching the CreateImage API call, recorded by CloudTrail, with an SNS topic target sends alerts with no code.
x.D: CloudTrail can't send logs directly to an SQS FIFO queue, and the Lambda function adds custom code.

x.A: Throttling on API Gateway rejects requests, so users would lose requests, which affects existing users.
x.B: DAX is a read cache and doesn't buffer writes to DynamoDB, so it wouldn't solve the write throughput problem.
x.C: A secondary index consumes more write capacity and doesn't fix write throttling.
x.D: An SQS queue buffers the requests durably, and Lambda writes them to DynamoDB at a rate it can sustain, so requests are not lost and existing users are not affected.

x.A: An interface endpoint can reach S3 privately, but it carries hourly and data charges and the application must use endpoint-specific DNS names. The gateway endpoint is the standard, free option that works with the normal S3 endpoint.
x.B: A gateway VPC endpoint for S3 keeps all API calls and data on the AWS network with no internet routing, and a bucket resource policy can restrict access to the instance's role.
x.C: S3 endpoints don't have private IP addresses that you can look up with nslookup, so a route to that address won't work.
x.D: The ip-ranges.json file lists public IP ranges, not private addresses, so routes made from it would still use public routes.

x.A: ElastiCache stores session data outside the instances, so any instance can read it. Sessions survive when instances scale in or out, which supports distributed session management.
x.B: Sticky sessions tie users to one instance, and if that instance is terminated during scale-in, the session is lost, so they aren't distributed.
x.C: Systems Manager Session Manager is for shell access to instances and doesn't manage application sessions.
x.D: GetSessionToken returns temporary AWS credentials and doesn't manage application session data.

x.A: Setting the minimum capacity to peak values wastes resources when traffic is lower, and CPU is a poor scaling signal here.
x.B: Creating extra Auto Scaling groups on demand via SNS is awkward and doesn't ensure no data is lost.
x.C: SQS queues buffer orders, but SQS notifications don't tell Auto Scaling how many instances are needed, so scaling on them isn't well matched to the workload.
x.D: Two SQS queues decouple collection and fulfillment, so no data is lost on scaling events. A backlog-per-instance metric scales each group to the amount of work, which optimizes resource usage.

x.A: CloudTrail records API activity, not an inventory of resources with a given tag.
x.B: Querying every service in every Region with the CLI is slow and means a lot of work.
x.C: CloudWatch Logs Insights queries log data and doesn't list tagged resources.
x.D: Resource Groups Tag Editor lets you search tagged resources across services and Regions in one query, which is the quickest way to find them.

x.A: Intelligent-Tiering fits variable access patterns that change rapidly. It keeps data immediately available with no retrieval fees and automatically moves data to cheaper tiers when it isn't being accessed.
x.B: Glacier Instant Retrieval charges retrieval fees, and with a rapidly changing access pattern it can cost more.
x.C: S3 Standard is available immediately but costs more than Intelligent-Tiering when parts of the data aren't accessed.
x.D: Standard-IA has retrieval fees and a minimum storage duration, so frequent access to some of the data costs more.

x.A: AWS WAF is a managed service that filters traffic to an ALB for common attacks like cross-site scripting and SQL injection, so there are no servers to manage.
x.B: Hosting on S3 with public access doesn't protect an ALB, and the application would need to be redesigned.
x.C: Shield Advanced protects against DDoS attacks, not application-level attacks like XSS and SQL injection.
x.D: A third-party firewall on EC2 is a server you must manage, patch, and scale, which goes against the goal of reducing responsibility.

x.A: EMR with Spark needs a cluster and a custom application, which is a lot of development and operations.
x.B: A Glue crawler discovers the CSV schema and a Glue ETL job converts to Parquet and writes it to the destination bucket. It is serverless and needs very little code.
x.C: AWS Batch with Bash needs a script to convert to Parquet, which means a lot more development.
x.D: A Lambda function would need code to convert to Parquet and may hit time or memory limits with large files, so it's more development effort.

x.A: At 500 Mbps, 700 TB would take far longer than a month online, but Snowball devices move it offline within the time. A lifecycle policy then moves it to Deep Archive, the lowest-cost class for infrequently accessed data kept 7 years.
x.B: A VPN runs over the same internet link, and 700 TB at that bandwidth takes longer than a month. Copying directly to Glacier also isn't the same as the lowest-cost path here.
x.C: A 500 Mbps Direct Connect would still take too long for 700 TB, and it takes time to provision and costs extra.
x.D: DataSync would use the 500 Mbps internet link, and 700 TB would take much longer than a month.

x.A: Downloading and re-uploading millions of objects is slow and a lot of effort.
x.B: Turning on default encryption covers future objects. S3 Inventory lists unencrypted objects, and an S3 Batch Operations copy job encrypts the existing objects at scale with little effort.
x.C: Changing the bucket's encryption settings only affects new objects. Existing objects stay unencrypted, and versioning doesn't encrypt them.
x.D: The console can't do bulk encryption of millions of objects through the Modify button, so it isn't practical.

x.A: A pilot-light style design with the infrastructure elements in place, Route 53 active-passive failover, and an Aurora Replica in another Region meets 30 minutes of downtime and data loss without running full capacity.
x.B: Active-active failover would send traffic to the second Region even when the primary is healthy, but the question says the secondary does not need to handle load.
x.C: A full replica and an Aurora database restored from the latest snapshot would have more data loss and active-active routing isn't needed.
x.D: Aurora doesn't support a second primary instance in another Region in this way, and rebuilding from backups can take longer than 30 minutes.

x.A: Security groups are stateful, so an inbound rule that allows TCP 443 from anywhere lets users reach the web server, and responses are allowed automatically.
x.B: A security group rule's destination applies to outbound traffic. It doesn't open inbound access from the internet.
x.C: Network ACLs are stateless, so allowing only inbound 443 isn't enough, because the response traffic would be blocked.
x.D: Allowing 443 both ways ignores that responses go back from the server to the client's ephemeral ports, not port 443.
x.E: Because network ACLs are stateless, you need an inbound rule for 443 and an outbound rule for the ephemeral port range for the responses.

x.A: T3 instances are burstable and not suited to sustained in-memory workloads, and making changes in the console isn't repeatable.
x.B: Manually raising capacity doesn't fit a stateful application, and more M5 instances don't give more memory per instance.
x.C: R5 instances are memory optimized, but CloudWatch doesn't provide built-in EC2 memory metrics, so the capacity planning approach described won't work.
x.D: R5 memory-optimized instances suit in-memory tasks, and changing the CloudFormation templates keeps the deployment repeatable. The CloudWatch agent can report memory and custom latency metrics.

x.A: A Glue job is for ETL and has a startup time that is too slow for results within a few seconds.
x.B: Lambda runs only when invoked, so you pay nothing during hours without requests. It starts quickly and handles asynchronous processing within seconds.
x.C: EKS runs a control plane and nodes continuously, so it costs money even when there are no requests.
x.D: ECS on EC2 has instances running constantly, which costs more when there are long idle periods.

x.A: An EBS volume attaches to one instance at a time and costs more per GB, so the reporting tool can't access all files concurrently.
x.B: EFS can be mounted by many clients at once but costs much more than S3 for 7 years of logs.
x.C: Instance store is temporary and is lost when the instance stops, so it can't retain logs for 7 years.
x.D: S3 is the lowest cost for long-term storage, is highly durable, and lets many readers access the files concurrently.

x.A: A cross-account IAM role in the company's account that trusts the vendor's role gives the vendor's tool temporary, least-privilege access without creating users or sharing credentials.
x.B: Creating an IAM user with a password for an automated tool is less secure and creates long-term credentials.
x.C: An IAM group in the company's account can't contain a user from another account.
x.D: The AWS account isn't an identity provider type you can add that way, so this isn't a valid approach.

x.A: An IAM role for the pod (for example through IAM roles for service accounts) gives the application temporary credentials with the permissions to write to DynamoDB.
x.B: An IAM user brings long-term credentials that must be stored and managed, which is less secure than a role.
x.C: A network ACL that allows outbound traffic doesn't provide a private path, and it doesn't stop traffic from going over the internet.
x.D: A VPC endpoint for DynamoDB gives private connectivity from the private subnets without going over the internet.
x.E: Embedding access keys in code is insecure and a bad practice.

x.A: A failover policy sends traffic to a primary resource and only uses the secondary if the primary fails, so traffic doesn't reach all running instances randomly.
x.B: A weighted policy sends traffic by assigned proportions and isn't random across all instances. It also has less health-aware behavior than multivalue.
x.C: A multivalue answer policy returns several healthy records chosen at random, so traffic reaches all running instances randomly, and unhealthy ones are left out.
x.D: Three instances split two and one across AZs leaves an unequal distribution, so losing the AZ with two instances removes most capacity.
x.E: Four instances split evenly across two AZs keep balanced capacity and stay available if one AZ fails.

x.A: A Kinesis stream that delivers to S3 doesn't give SQL on its own, and a data stream needs a consumer to deliver to S3. It is more setup than Firehose, and the data isn't directly queryable.
x.B: Firehose delivers data into a Redshift cluster, which scales to petabytes and lets teams run on-demand SQL analytics over existing and new data. Firehose is fully managed.
x.C: S3 with a Lambda function on arrival processes data but doesn't give SQL analytics, and it requires code.
x.D: EC2 ingestion with RDS is not designed for petabytes of analytics data and has the highest operational overhead.
